attacks.claim: The weekly public CC-BY export publishes per-response ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified and created_at. Removing resident_id does not anonymize: small-cell quasi-identifier combinations are near-unique, especially in small wards. There is no k-anonymity threshold, suppression, or aggregation, and a public release cannot be recalled.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Demographics that verified residents gave for jury-pool-style balance reports are reused and publicly released alongside political rankings. This is a purpose change with no consent, notice or privacy review, and it contradicts the anonymous-first, optional-verification constraint.
attacks.evidence: "collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports"

attacks.claim: Buying the county voter file and sending automated SMS plus 3 reminders to ~142,000 registered voters who never opted in is likely a TCPA violation, with statutory per-message damages, and risks carrier 10DLC and Twilio suspension. Twilio's default STOP handling does not cure missing consent. The sends are irreversible and have no kill switch, pilot cohort or throttling.
attacks.evidence: "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) with a link to the first poll, then 3 automated reminders over 10 days." / "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out."

attacks.claim: Voter registration files are commonly restricted by state law or Clerk terms to election or government purposes. The plan never checks permitted use, and it schedules the SMS and import pipeline into Week 4 with no legal or privacy review gate. It also creates a large new store of personal data (phone numbers) with no retention, access-control or deletion policy.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)." / ABSENT: legal review, permitted-use check, retention/deletion for voter file

attacks.claim: Integrity controls are weak. Device fingerprints and IPs are trivially rotated, and over-limit unverified responses are only queued, with no reviewer, SLA, capacity or alerting. It is unspecified whether queued responses count in the 'all responses' tally. Ward is self-selected for unverified users, so per-ward IRV can be manipulated, especially with mass SMS reach.
attacks.evidence: "unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review." / "ward is self-selected for unverified users"

attacks.claim: No retention or deletion policy exists for poll_responses or resident demographics. Staff cannot delete responses and no resident deletion or correction path is described.
attacks.evidence: "Staff cannot edit or delete responses" / ABSENT: retention and deletion policy

attacks.claim: The plan's own survey shows only 9% want polls, while the top requests (61% see council votes and reasons, 44% neighborhood notifications) are omitted. Ward Voice is still made the roadmap centerpiece with no evidence it serves the mission. The success metrics measure response volume and new-user share, not meaningful participation or council influence, and can be met by SMS blasting.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs "is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap"; "6,000 poll responses in the first 30 days."

attacks.claim: Ranking is specified as drag or tap-to-rank with no keyboard or screen-reader alternative, and accessibility is deferred to a Week 5 pass alongside the load test and launch. This is a public civic tool aimed at a broad audience.
attacks.evidence: "Week 2: resident ranking UI (mobile-first, drag or tap-to-rank)." / "Week 5: accessibility pass, load test"

attacks.claim: IRV semantics are unspecified for ties, exhausted ballots and partial rankings. There is no input validation or sanitization for options and rankings stored as jsonb, which are rendered in the results page and CSV/PDF, creating XSS and CSV-formula-injection risk. Server-side enforcement of opens_at/closes_at is not stated.
attacks.evidence: "results are shown per ward with instant-runoff tallies." / "options jsonb"

attacks.claim: The live IRV results page has no caching or precompute strategy, yet the SMS blast could drive heavy read load. The week-4 slot (export, PDF, import, SMS) plus a week-5 load test and launch has no contingency for a 3-person team.
attacks.evidence: "Live results page: instant-runoff rounds"; "Week 4: open-data export, staff PDF, voter-file import + SMS pipeline."

attacks.claim: SMS cost (~568k messages plus carrier fees) is not budgeted; only the $400 file cost is listed. The Twilio dependency has no DPA or exit path.
attacks.evidence: "$400, includes mobile numbers" / ABSENT: Twilio cost estimate
